items.title: Is AI destroying the art and magic of children's books?
items.excerpt: AI-generated 'slop' picture books are flooding online storefronts, and Creative Bloq talks to illustrators and parents about what happens to the craft of children's book illustration when generated art becomes the cheapest option. The piece looks at the tells of AI picture books and at the publishers and buyers trying to filter them out.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: children's picture book illustration + AI slop, from a design outlet (off-list; no on-list source covered the illustration-craft side in window).

items.title: Academic Publishers Develop Guidelines, Screening Tools for AI Use
items.excerpt: Just as booksellers are inundated with AI slop and trade publishing reckons with suspicions of AI-written books, academic publishing is building vetting tools and author guidelines for AI use. Publishers Lunch argues the scholarly side's screening infrastructure can inform how trade houses handle submissions.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: academic/scholarly screening tooling as a template for trade publishing.

items.title: Guest Post — When Errors Become Consensus: Science's Self-Correction Can No Longer Keep Up
items.excerpt: From 19th-century beef tea to paper mills and generative AI, the challenge for scholarly publishing is no longer detection alone — it is preventing bad claims from becoming embedded knowledge. Taylor & Francis research-integrity lead Jason Hu argues correction workflows have to change.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: paper mills + genAI contamination of the published record (research-integrity workflow).

items.title: Guest Post — AI Can Find the Article. Can It Tell Which Version It Used?
items.excerpt: When AI agents retrieve and summarise scholarly texts, they routinely cannot tell a preprint from a version of record. The authors argue persistent identifiers and version metadata are now the load-bearing infrastructure for machine readers of published work.
items.note: Metadata/versioning angle — machine readers of books and papers.

items.title: AI Invades Religion Books on Amazon (study: 63% likely AI-written)
items.excerpt: A survey by AI detector Originality.ai of 2,034 paperback religion books on Amazon found 63% were likely written by AI, including around three-quarters of titles on Hinduism, Taoism and witchcraft. The study puts a category-level number on catalogue dilution.
items.note: Category-specific study (religion shelf), distinct from generic catalogue-dilution coverage.

items.title: U.S. Textbook Authors Sue OpenAI for Copyright Infringement
items.excerpt: Textbook authors argue that if LLMs keep ingesting new editions as they appear, instructors and schools may drop textbook adoptions in favour of AI 'substitutes' — putting educational publishing's core product at risk, not just its copyright.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: educational/textbook publishing, adoption economics rather than generic copyright news.

items.title: Harriman House claims trade publishing first with 'AI-facilitated' Raoul Pal book
items.excerpt: Harriman House says The Everything Code, by macro analyst Raoul Pal, was produced with a proprietary AI tool trained exclusively on the author's own existing work — which the publisher calls a trade publishing first for an author-trained model in the manuscript pipeline.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: named production workflow — author-trained model used to build a trade book.

items.title: New manga platform features 300 titles translated into English for first time
items.excerpt: Shueisha's Manga Million puts nearly 300 previously untranslated titles into English plus Spanish, French, Turkish and Polish — a translation volume no human-only pipeline has attempted, and one readers and letterers have publicly questioned over uncredited translators and machine output.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: manga localisation at machine scale (translation labour + credit).

items.title: News Summary: Survey Suggests Many Publishers Still Fail to Register Copyright
items.excerpt: An Authors Guild survey found publishers had failed to register authors' copyrights, leaving some writers ineligible for the Anthropic settlement class — a paperwork failure that decides who gets paid when books are used as training data.
items.note: Practical consequence for authors; also covers audiobook company growth.

items.title: Andrea Bartz Returns to Ballantine for AI-Inspired Thriller
items.excerpt: Ballantine bought Delete Your Account by Andrea Bartz — the plaintiff in Bartz v. Anthropic — a novel about an author who has a chatbot write a book in the vein of her favourite thriller, with disastrous consequences.
items.note: NEW ANGLE: generative fiction as subject matter; AI-lawsuit plaintiff turns the story into a novel.
